raw:
{
  "need": "Identity",
  "secondary": { "name": "Competence", "note": "The shutdown often masks a fear of not being able to figure it out — avoidance is easier than admitting the path feels unclear." },
  "read": "Almost-18 means they are standing right at the edge of having to declare who they are becoming, and every college conversation feels like a referendum on that. The shutdown is not laziness — it is self-protection. If they never engage, they never have to risk being wrong or disappointing you. Status is tangled in here too: being asked to have answers they do not have yet makes them feel like a kid who is behind, not a capable person on the verge of adulthood.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Enforcer", "instinct": "Keep pushing — ask pointed questions, remind them of deadlines, maybe sit them down for a serious talk — which signals that you do not trust them to handle this on their own and turns every future conversation into a confrontation they want to escape." },
  "mentorMove": "Stop making college the subject and make them the subject — their interests, what they find meaningful, who they want to be around. The expectation stays: you are going to figure out a next step together. But you approach it sideways, as someone genuinely curious about their inner world, not a deadline enforcer.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "Having a plan — any real, thought-through plan — by graduation is the standard. Gap year, trade program, community college, four-year school, all on the table, but drifting without intention is not.",
    "They engage with the conversation. Shutting down is not an option you accept long-term, even if the pace is slower than you would like."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "When and where the conversation happens — a drive, a walk, over food — anywhere that is not face-to-face at the kitchen table feels less like an interrogation.",
    "What the plan actually looks like. You are not attached to a specific path, only to the fact that they own one."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 2, "label": "Questions" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I want to be honest with you about something. I've noticed that every time college or next year comes up, you go quiet or change the subject, and I've been doing it wrong — I've been leading with logistics when I haven't actually asked you what's going on inside about all of it. That's on me." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "So I'm asking now, for real — not about applications or deadlines — just: when you picture life at 20, what does it feel like? Not what it looks like, just the feeling. And what part of this whole thing feels the most murky right now?" },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "I hear that. And I want you to know I am not trying to steer you toward one answer — I genuinely don't care whether it's a big university or a two-year program or something else entirely, as long as it's something you've actually thought through and can get behind. What if we just spent some time — no pressure, no forms open — mapping out what matters to you, and we figure out what fits that?" },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I am going to hold you to having a real plan before you graduate. Not because I'm anxious about it, but because I have high standards for you and I know you are more than capable of building a life with intention — you just need space to think it through on your own terms. I'm not going anywhere, and neither is the expectation. But I'd rather be someone you think out loud with than someone you're hiding from." }
  ],
  "longGame": "The goal is not a college application — it is a kid who learns to sit with uncertainty and move through it rather than freeze. If you can become the person they actually talk to about this, you have won something bigger than any enrollment deadline. Keep the standard visible and keep yourself safe to approach, and they will get there."
}
situation: My almost-18-year-old shuts down every time college or life after graduation comes up.
